I think that in order for this article to be particularly relevant, it would have had to mention the impact of having one of the Yogscast (Sjin) feature the game early in the early access process and then again throughout development. You may have heard of another indie title featured regularly by a Yogscast member (Duncan)...Kerbal Space Program. When we're talking about games in the Steam 'Early Access' program, few things can provide the developers with a substantial cash infusion like having the game promo'd to 100k-200k people 10-20 episodes at a stretch. (The last episode in Sjin's first series featuring the game back in 2013 has 360k views). If 1 in every 1000 people to watch any given episode were to wander over to Steam and bought the game for $30, it would translate to hundreds of thousands of dollars for the developer to fund continued development.

That's kind of a big deal.

Fair is far; Introversion did a good job throughout development and launched a game that they and their players were happy with. We just can't underestimate the impact of regular, substantial cash infusions throughout the development process to help keep the developers focused more on how to fix that pesky bug or properly implement that cool feature than on whether or not they're going to make rent this month.

One of the things about the Early Access program that lots of people completely overlook is what happens when developers get a game into the Early Access program but don't generate enough revenue from it to keep themselves going. People think that just because you're in the Early Access program that you're getting tons of money but we know now that nothing could be farther from the truth. The average game on Steam sells 32k copies and developing through the Early Access program alone isn't showing any influence on improving that.

The chances of a studio staying funded through the development process is related in large part to the scope of promotional coverage they receive. A developer can do all the things listed in this article and still run out of cash long before the game sees completion. Younger readers won't necessarily appreciate the magnitude of the situation but adult readers all know that the landlord/bank, the utility companies, and the grocery store don't pro-rate their prices because your Early Access game didn't shift enough units this month for you to draw enough of a salary to live on. There's enormous risk in spending resources to make a game when you have very few resources to spend and both developers and Early Access buyers need to be crystal clear on this.
